extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and project teams preparing Funding Inquiries/proposals to the John Templeton Foundation Religion, Science, & Society funding area (2026 cycle)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing a 3-year research funding inquiry/proposal for the John Templeton Foundation's Religion, Science, & Society funding area (2026), targeting one of the three topical areas: Intelligence, Meaning Making, or Imagined Futures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with funding area scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should address fundamental questions about human existence, how people can flourish and find meaning, and how societies envision the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Religion, Science, & Society funding area will not consider inquiries unrelated to the research areas listed. Recognizing overlap among topics, apply to the topical area that best fits your proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project duration and cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: For the 2026 funding cycle, the Foundation invites three-year projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit an Online Funding Inquiry by the deadline (July 15, 2026) through the Templeton Portal/OFI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary activity must be research
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals may include components aimed at public engagement, but the primary activities of the project must be research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public engagement can be a component but should not supplant research as the project's main activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary teams prioritized
rubrics_metrics.description: The Foundation prioritizes projects composed of interdisciplinary teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdisciplinarity should be reflected in project personnel, activities, outputs, and framing; cross-disciplinary collaboration is encouraged across the topical areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical-area fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply to the specific topical area (Intelligence, Meaning Making, or Imagined Futures) that best fits the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should be submitted under the correct OFI selection (e.g., 'Religion, Science, and Society – Special Topic', 'Meaning Making', or 'Imagined Futures').

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence topical alignment with venture themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should apply theological, philosophical, and social scientific approaches to the guiding themes outlined in the Foundation-wide Intelligence Venture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should engage questions such as uniqueness of human intelligence, alternative kinds of intelligence, and broader metaphysical or ontological implications as framed by the Intelligence Venture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify and interrogate conception of intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must specify and interrogate the conception of intelligence they engage (human, divine, or arising from other domains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state which concept(s) of intelligence the project uses and critically examine that conception within the project's methods and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability of insights (Intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects should offer transferable insights across historical settings, disciplines, and confessional communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design work so findings or frameworks can be applied beyond a narrowly bounded case or tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative depth vs focused single-tradition work (Intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects may compare multiple theological and philosophical approaches or focus deeply on one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both comparative and deep single-tradition studies are acceptable; justify the chosen scope and how it advances understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with tech, business, and arts (Intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage projects that engage partners and communities in tech, business, and arts to introduce existential and philosophical questions into new spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partnerships beyond academia are valued for broadening impact and applicability of findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative methodologies (Intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop innovative methodologies that shed new light on classical debates or reveal fresh dimensions of canonical texts and traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological innovation—new analytic tools, digital humanities techniques, experimental designs—strengthens proposals that revisit classical materials or debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requested budget ranges (Intelligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: We welcome projects ranging from small, focused studies (less than $260K) to larger collaborative initiatives (up to $2.5M), including use of subgrants or RFP structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select budget request consistent with project scope; large projects employing competitive subgrants should justify RFP/subgrant mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on concrete manifestations (Meaning Making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate concrete manifestations of meaning making in a world marked by rapid social change, attending to practices, experiences, and transitions that enable people to develop, sustain, or renew a life of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should target specific dimensions of life (e.g., parenting, vocation, play) or particular tensions (agency vs constraint, mystery vs meaninglessness, suffering vs joy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention potential and clarification of conditions (Meaning Making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive proposals will demonstrate potential to intervene constructively in tensions and clarify the conditions in specific spheres that support meaning making and beneficial outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize how research could inform practical interventions, policies, or community practices that foster resilience, fulfillment, or social/spiritual attunement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary integration (Meaning Making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate the sciences with philosophy, theology, or religious studies through robust interdisciplinary collaboration as reflected in personnel, activities, outputs, and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show concrete plans for interdisciplinary work—roles, methods, shared outputs—that bridge analytic and interpretive approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralistic relevance (Meaning Making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce findings relevant to pluralistic societies and individuals who may or may not claim religious affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame questions and outputs so they speak to diverse belief backgrounds and civic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual and contextual clarity (Meaning Making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a novel approach to a well-defined setting or tension to ensure conceptual and contextual clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly diffuse scopes; clearly define setting, population, or tension and explain how the approach is novel and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requested budget ranges and structures (Meaning Making)
rubrics_metrics.description: This topical area considers projects between $700K and $1.5M; projects over $1M should use an RFP structure for competitively selected subgrants; focused studies requesting less than $260K are also considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose request size consistent with project design; use RFP/subgrant structure when proposing large, distributed programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthening future-imagination capacity (Imagined Futures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek to strengthen the capacity of communities and societies to envision and navigate the future, examining how religious, philosophical, and narrative traditions inform imagination and possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should clarify how traditions and cultural resources shape foresight, planning, and orientation toward future possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and interpretive methods (Imagined Futures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use empirical and interpretive methods to examine evolutionary, cognitive, and cultural processes shaping the human capacity to think about and prepare for the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological pluralism is appropriate—combine qualitative, interpretive, and empirical tools to illuminate how communities structure time and foresight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods producing predictive and scenario insights (Imagined Futures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive proposals should employ methods capable of generating predictive insights, imaginative scenarios, and future-oriented knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches may range from computational/predictive models to theoretical and interpretive inquiries; ensure methods are fit to produce the claimed foresight outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quantitative and computational techniques (Imagined Futures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches may include statistical methods, demographic projections, agent-based simulations, and mathematical models to enhance understanding of future mental states, practices, behaviors, and cultural innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using such techniques, explain model assumptions, validation strategies, and how quantitative outputs will be interpreted alongside qualitative insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary expertise including humanities and media studies (Imagined Futures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw on expertise from the humanities and media studies alongside the social sciences, theology, or philosophy, as reflected in the project team and partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams should show how varied disciplinary perspectives contribute to analytic and communicative goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrative 'generative juxtapositions' (Imagined Futures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate generative juxtapositions—such as empirical methods and narrative analysis, wisdom traditions and contemporary media, or philosophical inquiry and popular culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals that creatively combine different framings and methods to generate new insights about futures are encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential to inform institutional preparedness and response (Imagined Futures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate clear potential to inform how institutions, communities, or societies prepare for and respond to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate pathways from research findings to institutional or community practices, policies, or planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requested budget ranges and project scale (Imagined Futures)
rubrics_metrics.description: This topical area will prioritize exploratory projects with a request amount of up to $260K and clear, achievable outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clear deliverables and achievable scope when requesting smaller exploratory grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural submission requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Interested applicants must register and submit a Funding Inquiry at the Templeton Portal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Foundation's OFI/portal processes and select the correct topical area when applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not submit unrelated inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The funding area will not consider inquiries unrelated to the listed research areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a project does not meaningfully engage the specified topical areas or research emphases, it is unlikely to be considered.
